title: Books Aren't Disappearing From Schools
author: The Next 30 Years
summary: Analyzing a new RAND report on whole-book reading in secondary English classrooms, this article finds that the 'novels have vanished' panic is overstated -- 90% of secondary ELA teachers assign at least one full fiction or nonfiction book per year -- but the more troubling finding is an equity gap: students in high-poverty schools, majority-nonwhite schools, and those with disabilities are consistently assigned fewer books. The RAND report also finds that teachers using publisher-developed materials assign fewer books than those using self-created materials, but the article argues the real driver is not publishers but the accountability systems that shaped their products. For at least 25 years, high-stakes reading tests have imposed a theory of literacy as transferable skills demonstrated on short decontextualized passages; publishers aligned to what tests reward. This 'skills and strategies' approach conflicts with the science of reading's emphasis on background knowledge, vocabulary, and fluency. Whole books matter because they build cognitive persistence -- sustained attention and the ability to remain immersed in language over time -- in ways that excerpt-driven practice cannot. Doug Lemov: whole books cultivate 'cognitive persistence' that is becoming increasingly rare in fragmented digital culture. Mike Austin: books invite students into an ongoing cultural and moral conversation larger than themselves.
points: * 90% of secondary ELA teachers assign at least one full book per year, contradicting the 'novels have disappeared' narrative -- but the equity finding is more troubling: disadvantaged students, multilingual learners, and students with disabilities are consistently assigned fewer books. * Publisher-developed curricula assign fewer books than teacher-created materials, but the real driver is the accountability system: high-stakes tests impose a fragmented theory of reading as transferable skills on short passages, and curricula align to what tests reward. * Reading a book is not just extended passage reading -- it requires different cognitive habits: sustained attention, memory, fluency, and the ability to remain immersed in language and ideas over long stretches of time. * Doug Lemov: whole books cultivate 'cognitive persistence' that is becoming increasingly rare in digital culture; this is precisely what the excerpt-driven skills approach cannot build. * Mike Austin: books welcome students into an ongoing cultural and moral conversation larger than themselves -- whole books matter not merely because they are long but because they allow students to inhabit another consciousness deeply enough to encounter enduring human questions.
quotes: RAND brings something refreshing to the conversation: evidence. And, as it tends to do, the evidence complicates nearly everyone's preferred narrative.

reading a book is not just an extended version of reading a passage. It requires different cognitive habits: sustained attention, memory, fluency, and the ability to remain immersed in language and ideas over long stretches of time.
teaching whole books effectively means cultivating 'cognitive persistence' in ways that are becoming increasingly rare in our fragmented digital culture.
the students most in need of the benefits that whole books provide appear least likely to receive them.
the accountability era has normalized a fragmented theory of reading across the entire K-12 system.
Books welcome students into an ongoing cultural and moral conversation larger than themselves.
reading tests damage reading instruction: they subtly teach educators to think about reading in ways that are at odds with cognitive science.
